title: Effects of Popular Science Writing Instruction on General Education Student Attitudes Towards Science: A Case Study in Astronomy
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a writing-intensive introductory astronomy seminar for non-STEM undergraduates can improve students’ attitudes toward science and their confidence in engaging with scientific material. The authors are interested in whether popular science writing can serve as a useful instructional strategy for general education students, especially those outside STEM majors, by helping them see science as more relevant, understandable, and accessible.

The intervention took place in a third-quarter seminar within a year-long freshman general education science program at a large public university in the United States. In the course, students worked through scaffolded writing projects centered on astrobiology and science journalism, including translating a research article for a lay audience, drafting a popular science piece, keeping a writing journal, and completing related reading and in-class activities. The study used pre- and post-course surveys with Likert-scale and open-ended questions, plus follow-up interviews with a small subset of students. The qualitative analysis focused on changes in attitudes toward astronomy, science relevance, perceptions of scientists, and confidence in tasks such as reading research articles, explaining science, and writing about a discovery.

The study found generally positive changes in students’ confidence and attitudes, especially for reading scientific articles, explaining science concepts, and writing about science. Students also reported a broader view of who can participate in science and greater appreciation of communication, ethics, and accessibility as important scientific skills. However, many attitudes were already positive at baseline, especially regarding the value and relevance of science. The authors conclude that writing-focused science instruction can help non-major undergraduates feel more capable of engaging with science and can broaden their conception of science beyond professional research careers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative pre/post case study without a control group, randomization, or delayed follow-up. It offers useful process evidence, but it does not meet stronger causal-comparison criteria for K-12 intervention claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are positive but modest and largely self-reported, with no effect sizes, no control condition, and no evidence on durability or transfer. The study suggests promise for writing-focused science instruction, but only under the narrow condition of a small, selective, writing-intensive non-majors astronomy seminar rather than the broader AI/science-reasoning thesis.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study reports that the writing-intensive astronomy seminar improved students’ science writing confidence and helped them better read and synthesize scientific sources. In matched pre/post responses, 9/15 students reported improved attitudes toward reading scientific research articles, and 9 students felt more confident about writing about a new scientific discovery; no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Matched pre/post open-ended survey responses and interviews about reading research articles, reading popular science writing, and writing about a new scientific discovery
finding.study_size: n=19 survey respondents; qualitative coding shown for n=13-15 matched respondents in figures

finding.finding_summary: Students reported improved ability to understand how science works, interpret scientific articles, and connect evidence to claims after the course’s writing-focused assignments. The paper emphasizes that translating primary articles and writing for lay audiences forced students to grasp scientific content more deeply, but it does not report a controlled effect size or delayed post-test.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about understanding science, reading primary literature, and explaining scientific concepts; descriptive ASSA/EBAPS survey summaries

finding.finding_summary: The strongest reported gains were in students’ confidence and comfort engaging with science tasks, especially reading research articles, explaining science concepts, and writing about discoveries. The paper states that 9/15 students reported improved attitudes toward reading scientific articles, 9 became more confident in explaining science, and 9 felt more confident about writing a new discovery; quantitative ASSA changes were descriptive and not significant at p<0.05.
finding.measure: Confidence/comfort ratings and coded open-ended responses about engaging with science tasks
finding.study_size: n=19 survey respondents; matched coding figures show n=14-15 for specific items

finding.finding_summary: The course increased students’ self-reported ability to communicate science, think critically about science news, and connect science to humanities-oriented interests. Students described writing as improving synthesis, audience awareness, and critical consumption of science media, but the study is qualitative and does not include a transfer task or delayed assessment.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey coding and interviews on communicating science, audience awareness, and critical engagement with science news

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports improved attitudes toward astronomy content and science relevance in a non-majors general-education course. Descriptively, the authors note increased interest in astronomy/general science and improved perceptions of the relevance and benefits of science, but they do not provide a causal comparison with a control group or a delayed post-test.
finding.measure: ASSA category scores and open-ended responses on interest in astronomy and relevance/benefits of science
finding.study_size: n=19 survey respondents; descriptive figure summaries show n=13-15 matched responses
